Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The equation used to convert the measured quantities into an age or date, together with a citation for that equation.
Name the equation unambiguously; where a procedure supports more than one, state which is used and under what conditions.

Reason: external reporting standards require it — provenance, not our Column C (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by every geochronology reporting standard surveyed (Condon et al. 2024; Schaen et al. 2021; Rooney et al. 2024; Flowers et al. 2024; Kohn et al. 2024; Mahan et al. 2023).
Distinct from Age Model and Software, which records how multiple analyses are combined into a single reported result.
The kind of date or age the procedure reports.

Reason: why a bare age is ambiguous
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Most dating systems derive several different date types from the same measurements, so a reported age is ambiguous without this.
Where more than one type is reported, list all, separated by semicolons.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Kohn et al. (2024) carry this as a named required item ("fission-track age type"); the equivalent distinction is required by all five other standards surveyed.
How any non-radiogenic, inherited or pre-existing component of the measured signal was accounted for, including the composition assumed, its source, and its uncertainty.
Record 'None' where the measured quantity accumulates from zero and no such component exists.

Reason: scope rationale — which dating systems it applies to
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Applies to five of the six dating systems surveyed; fission track is the sole genuine exception, as tracks accumulate from zero.

Reason: the sentence exists to justify the D tier; that is what Column D encodes
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: D=Editable rather than Read-Only: the procedure registers the correction method and any default composition, but the value actually applied is frequently sample-specific (a two-stage model composition is evaluated at the interpreted age) or session-derived (a trapped composition solved from an isochron intercept), and a revision to the assumed composition should not require registering a new procedure.

Reason: library-internal design cross-reference to Rule 5
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Same reasoning as Rule 5's Constants and Reference Values Used.
The proportion of the measured signal that is radiogenic, as opposed to inherited, initial or otherwise non-radiogenic.

Reason: 'records what the session actually produced' restates C=N/A; the companion boundary is real
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Measured companion to Inherited or Initial Signal Correction, which is procedure-level: this field records what the session actually produced.

Reason: why the fraction matters for interpreting the age
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: It indicates how strongly the reported age depends on the assumed non-radiogenic composition — a result derived from a low radiogenic fraction is sensitive to that assumption in a way a high-fraction result is not, and that sensitivity is invisible from the age and its uncertainty alone.

Reason: library-internal design note — criterion-versus-measurement split
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Follows the criterion-versus-measurement split used for Oxide Production.
The statistical model used to combine individual analyses into a single reported age, including any criteria governing which model is applied.

Reason: why the model choice changes the result
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is a methodological choice that changes the result: a Model-1 and a Model-3 regression of the same data yield different ages and different uncertainties.

Record the model only — the software implementing it belongs in Data Reduction Software (Group 3), whose scope already extends to age calculation; where reduction and age regression use different packages, list both there.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required in some form by all six geochronology reporting standards surveyed.
The zero point from which the reported age is measured, where this is not the present day, and the date it corresponds to.
Record 'Present day' where the conventional datum applies.

Reason: external requirement plus concrete per-system instructions
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Explicitly required wherever the datum is not the present: year of sample collection for luminescence (Mahan et al. 2023), end of irradiation for 40Ar/39Ar decay corrections (Schaen et al. 2021).

The rules determining which individual analyses contribute to a reported aggregate result, together with the outcome of applying them: how many analyses were acquired, how many were included, and on what grounds any were excluded.
Distinct from within-analysis outlier filtering, which removes anomalous points inside a single analysis: this field decides which whole analyses enter the reported value.

Reason: design rationale for combining criteria and outcome
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Criteria and outcome are combined in one field because neither is interpretable without the other, following the precision/accuracy precedent.
The statistic reported to show whether scatter among the contributing analyses exceeds what analytical uncertainty alone predicts, together with its value.

Reason: what the statistic answers
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Answers whether a reported aggregate is defensible as a single population.

Reason: explains C=N/A explicitly, then adds a real boundary about the threshold
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure-level tier is N/A because the value cannot be known before the analysis; the procedure may still state an acceptance threshold, which belongs with the inclusion criteria.
The rules governing which part of the sample is analysed, and why.
Covers the criteria applied when choosing grains, aliquots, spots, or a region of interest — size, morphology, clarity, freedom from inclusions or alteration, phase identity, or spatial position.
Distinct from Target Material, which states the material type the procedure is designed for: this field states how, within such a sample, the analysed portion is picked out.

Imaging or other characterisation performed before the measurement in order to select or locate the analysed target, including the technique, instrument and settings used, and how individual analyses are linked back to the images.
Distinct from any imaging the procedure performs as its own measurement.
Where the imaging is performed on a separate instrument, it should also be recorded in the Group 1 coupling fields.

The chemical species this procedure is designed to determine, recorded at whatever resolution the chemistry is resolved — element(s) for this technique; valence species where a procedure resolves oxidation state; compounds where it resolves molecules.
Isotopes are not analytes: isotopes of an element are the same chemical species.

Reason: 'procedure registers the suite; at analysis level the analyst records the subset' is the C/D split
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The procedure registers the full analyte suite; at analysis level the analyst records the specific subset actually measured in the session, which may be narrower if species were excluded due to interferences or scope reduction.

Reason: restates what Column I encodes
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Fields whose Keyed By column declares 'analyte' apply individually to each entry in this list.

The measured level of the analytical blank in the session, and — where the reported quantity is a ratio — its composition, since a blank subtracted from a ratio biases the result unless its own composition is known.

Reason: 'records what was actually measured' restates D=Basic; the companion boundary is real
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Companion to the blank correction method, which is procedure-level: this field records what was actually measured.

Reason: library-internal design note
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Follows the criterion-versus-measurement split the library applies wherever a procedure sets a threshold and an analysis reports a value against it.
An externally-calibrated factor that converts the measured quantity into the reported quantity, how it was determined, and its uncertainty.
Applies where the conversion depends on a factor calibrated against a reference of independently known value, rather than on the instrument response alone.
Distinct from the fields that name the calibration material and that state which approach applies to which analyte, where the technique has them: this field records the resulting factor itself.
Description of the multi-collector Faraday cup array.

Specify the total number of Faraday cup detectors (fixed and moveable), their labeled positions (e.g., L4, L3, L2, L1, Ax, H1, H2, H3, H4 for a 9-cup Neptune), and the presence and position of any ion counter (SEM) or Daly detector in the collector block.

Reason: why cup count and span matter
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The number and span of cups constrains which isotope combinations can be simultaneously collected.
Resistance values (Ω) of the feedback resistors in the Faraday cup amplifiers.
Standard amplifiers use 10¹¹ Ω resistors, yielding 1 V per ~6.24 × 10⁶ ion counts per second.

Reason: why high-gain amplifiers are fitted
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: High-gain amplifiers (10¹² or 10¹³ Ω) are fitted to selected cups to improve signal-to-noise for very low-intensity beams (e.g., 234U, low-abundance spike isotopes).
Report the resistor value per cup position, or note 'all 10¹¹ Ω' if uniform.
Method used to calibrate the relative gain (amplification factor) of each Faraday cup amplifier at the start of or during each analytical session.

Reason: why gain differences must be corrected
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Relative gain differences between amplifiers cause systematic errors in isotope ratios if uncorrected.

Common approaches: instrument internal gain calibration routine (measures signal in each cup sequentially using a common beam), amplifier rotation procedure, or measurement of a known isotope ratio solution in each cup.
For instruments with SEM detectors, also describes the SEM-to-Faraday cross-calibration sequence.
Specify frequency (per session, per block, weekly).
Assignment of isotope masses to Faraday cup or ion counter detector positions for this procedure, and the analyte each position serves.
Lists the mass number monitored in each collector position with its analyte element where it has one — e.g. 'L3=116Sn (Sn); L2=117Sn (Sn); Ax=120Sn (Sn); H1=121Sb (interference monitor, no analyte)'.

Interference-monitor and internal-standard positions serve no analyte and carry no parent element; the analyte list itself is given by the Analyte field and is never inferred from the mass labels here.
For static multi-collection procedures, one configuration applies throughout the measurement.
For multi-dynamic procedures, list all configurations and the cycling sequence.

Reason: why assignments differ between element systems
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Different element systems require different mass assignments within the collector array span.
Number of measurement blocks acquired per sample or standard solution introduction.
In MC-ICP-MS, data are structured as blocks of cycles; each block typically begins with a baseline (on-peak zero) measurement before the analytical cycles.

Reason: why multiple blocks are useful
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Multiple blocks per sample allow inspection of signal stability and within-measurement drift.

Reason: 'procedure specifies; analyst may adjust' is the D=Editable definition
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard number; analyst may adjust for samples with low signal or for high-precision requirements.
Number of measurement cycles acquired per block.
One cycle corresponds to a single set of simultaneous Faraday cup readings integrated for the duration specified in Integration Time per Cycle.
Total integration time per sample = (Number of Cycles per Block) × (Integration Time per Cycle) × (Number of Blocks per Measurement).

Reason: as above
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard value; analyst may adjust within procedure bounds.
Duration of signal integration per measurement cycle (seconds).

Reason: what it determines
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Determines counting statistics per cycle.

Reason: the precision/drift trade-off
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Longer integration times improve shot-noise precision but increase the impact of signal drift within the integration window.

Reason: why high-gain channels need longer integration
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For high-gain (10¹² or 10¹³ Ω) amplifier channels, longer integration times are often required to accumulate sufficient charge.

Reason: as above
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard integration time; analyst may confirm or adjust within procedure bounds.
Where different isotope channels use different integration schemes, record the time for each channel.
Method and timing for measuring the ion beam baseline (on-peak zero) during acquisition, and the portion of the acquisition it is taken from.

Reason: enumerates the three approaches (definition) with the reason each applies (rationale)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Three approaches are in use and the choice depends on how sample reaches the plasma: deflecting the ion beam (beam-off or electrostatic deflector); aspirating an acid blank, which applies only to solution introduction; or, for laser ablation, collecting a defined number of laser-off cycles at the start of the same block, since no blank can be aspirated mid-ablation.
State which, and how many cycles or how long.
Mathematical law used to parameterize instrumental isotope mass fractionation as a function of mass difference.

Reason: why the exponential law is preferred
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The exponential law (Maréchal et al. 1999) is most widely used and theoretically best justified for MC-ICP-MS.
The linear law assumes fractionation proportional to mass difference.
The power law is an alternative formulation.
For double-spike procedures, the law is embedded in the inversion algorithm and must be consistent between spike calibration and sample data reduction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Element and isotope ratio used as the internal normalization standard for mass bias correction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Reason: mechanism — how the correction works
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The measured ratio of the normalizing element is used to calculate the mass bias factor β using the chosen mass fractionation law, which is then applied to correct the analyte isotope ratios assuming β_norm ≈ β_analyte.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Specify the element, the monitored isotope ratio (e.g., 113Cd/111Cd for Sb measurements), and the certified or consensus value used for correction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' if internal normalization is not used.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Reason: duplicates S4 almost exactly; one of the two must go
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' where the procedure does not use internal normalization.
The pair of enriched isotopes used to construct the double spike.

Reason: selection constraints plus the reason for them
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Both isotopes must be naturally rare, free from isobaric interferences, and chosen to minimize error magnification in the inversion.
The double spike composition must be accurately calibrated before use.
Specify both isotope masses and the spike certificate or calibration reference.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Reason: duplicates S5; one of the two must go
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' where the procedure does not use a double spike.
Target proportion of double-spike signal relative to total analyte signal in the spiked mixture, expressed as spike fraction (0–1) or spike:sample ratio.

Reason: why an optimum exists plus how it is determined
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: An optimal mixing ratio minimizes error propagation through the double-spike inversion; the optimum is analyte-system specific and is typically determined using the Double Spike Toolbox or equivalent.
The achieved mixing ratio may deviate from the target within acceptable bounds (typically ±20% of optimal); the double-spike inversion corrects for actual mixing ratios.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Reason: duplicates S4; one of the two must go
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' where the procedure does not use a double spike.
Mathematical algorithm used to simultaneously solve for the true sample isotope ratio and the mass fractionation factor from the measured spike-sample mixture.
Common implementations: iterative Newton-Raphson solution, matrix algebraic approach, or published software (e.g., Rudge et al. 2009 Double Spike Toolbox).
Specify the algorithm or software reference and version.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Reason: duplicates S4; one of the two must go
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' where the procedure does not use a double spike.
Method used to verify that every collector sits on a flat region of its peak top simultaneously, and the acceptance threshold applied before analysis begins.

Reason: why simultaneous collection makes peak flatness critical
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Specific to simultaneous collection: a sequential instrument centres one mass at a time, whereas a multi-collector array must have all cups on flat peak tops at once or the measured ratio carries a peak-shape bias that no downstream correction removes.
Typically assessed by scanning across the peak plateau, or by comparing ratios measured at slightly offset mass positions.
Peak flatness actually achieved in the session, assessed against the criterion registered by the procedure.

Reason: library-internal design note — criterion-versus-measurement split
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Companion measured value to Peak Flatness Method and Threshold, following the criterion-versus-measurement split used for Oxide Production.
Procedure applied immediately before each analysis to remove surface contamination or condition the sample surface.
Distinct from general sample preparation.
For spot analysis, pre-ablation pulses are discarded before signal acquisition begins.

Reason: guidance that it is omitted for mapping, plus the reason
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For mapping, this step is typically omitted as the large area ablated averages out surface effects.
Manufacturer and model of the laser ablation system.
Wavelength and type of the laser used for ablation in nanometres.
Type, design origin, and internal volume of the ablation cell.

Reason: why cell volume matters — washout and time resolution
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Cell volume is a primary determinant of aerosol washout time and therefore the achievable time resolution of the data.
Shape and dimensions of the laser ablation spot in micrometres registered by the procedure.
For circular spots, report diameter; for square or rectangular spots, report width × length.

Reason: 'procedure registers...analysts may adjust' is the D=Editable definition
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The procedure registers the typical geometry; analysts may adjust within procedure-allowed range.
Sampling mode or ablation pattern used during analysis.
Laser pulse energy in millijoules as set at the laser output or measured at the sample surface.

Reason: why energy is less useful than fluence
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Less commonly reported than fluence because it does not account for spot area.
Report only when the system displays energy directly.

Reason: cites 'Default Laser Fluence'; the field is named 'Laser Fluence (Energy Density)'
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Laser fluence (J cm⁻²) is the preferred quantity and is captured in Default Laser Fluence.
Laser pulse energy per unit area at the sample surface in J cm⁻², as registered by the procedure.

Reason: why fluence is the physically meaningful quantity
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Fluence is the physically meaningful quantity controlling ablation rate, crater morphology, elemental fractionation, and particle size distribution.
If the system reports only as % of maximum output, include that value and note the system maximum where known.
Spatial energy distribution of the laser beam at the sample surface, and whether a beam homogenizer is installed.

Reason: why flat-top beats Gaussian
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: A flat-top (top-hat) profile produces more uniform ablation craters and more reproducible crater morphology than a Gaussian beam.

Reason: 'fixed hardware property' is what D=Read-Only encodes
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is a fixed hardware property of the laser system.
Laser pulse repetition rate in hertz registered by the procedure.

Reason: how it combines with other settings to set resolution
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For mapping methods, repetition rate together with scan speed and spot size determines pixel size and spatial resolution.

Reason: 'analysts may adjust within bounds' is the D=Editable definition
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Analysts may adjust within procedure-allowed bounds.
Duration of each individual laser pulse, including units.

Reason: why ns vs fs changes the ablation regime
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Pulse duration determines the ablation regime: nanosecond (ns) pulses involve significant thermal effects and elemental fractionation; femtosecond (fs) pulses are non-thermal and substantially reduce elemental fractionation and matrix effects.

Reason: as above
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is a fixed hardware property of the laser system.
Total on-sample ablation (signal acquisition) time per individual spot in seconds, as set in the acquisition method.

Reason: 'this is a procedure-level parameter' restates C; the trade-off is the real content
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is a procedure-level parameter for spot analysis: it reflects the deliberate trade-off between signal accumulation (longer = lower LOD), sample consumption, and session throughput.
For transect analysis, the equivalent procedure-level parameter is scan speed (captured in Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size).

Reason: 'therefore analysis-level' restates the tier
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For mapping analysis, total acquisition time is sample-area-dependent and therefore analysis-level, not captured here.

Field: Ablation Pit Depth and Ablation Rate
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Depth of the ablation pit produced under the registered laser conditions, the method used to measure it, and the resulting per-pulse ablation rate.

Field: Ablation Pit Depth and Ablation Rate
Reason: what pit depth governs
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Sets the achievable depth resolution and governs downhole elemental fractionation.

Field: Ablation Pit Depth and Ablation Rate
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For transect and mapping the equivalent quantity is trench depth under the same conditions.
Diameter of the laser spot as independently measured on the sample or on a test material, distinct from the nominal value the procedure registers.

Reason: why a measured companion is needed — nominal and delivered differ
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Measured companion to Laser Spot Geometry: nominal and delivered spot size can differ appreciably with optics condition and focus.

Field: Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For continuous line scan (transect) and raster mapping: the stage translation speed in µm s⁻¹.

Field: Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size
Reason: 'the procedure-level parameter' restates C; the resolution relationship is the content
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is the procedure-level parameter that, together with spot size and repetition rate, determines spatial resolution along the scan direction.

Field: Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For mapping, the mapping rate (mm² h⁻¹) may be reported as an alternative when scan speed is session-variable.

Field: Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For stepped line profiles: the distance between successive spot positions in µm.
Distance between adjacent raster lines in a 2D elemental map, measured perpendicular to the scan direction, in micrometres.

Reason: why spacing relative to spot size matters
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Together with spot size, this determines whether adjacent lines are contiguous (line spacing = spot size), overlapping (line spacing < spot size), or have gaps (line spacing > spot size).
Applies to raster mapping only.
Total length of the transect line analysed in micrometres.

Reason: explicitly justifies the analysis-level tier
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is an analysis-level parameter because it depends on the size of the feature of interest rather than being fixed in the procedure.

Reason: 'determined at analysis time' restates D=Basic
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The procedure fixes scan speed (captured in Transect Rate, Mapping Rate or Step Size); transect length is determined at analysis time based on grain or feature size.
Location of the analysis on the sample surface.
For spot and transect analysis: stage coordinates (X, Y in µm) or a description relative to a named reference feature (e.g., mineral rim, inclusion boundary).
For mapping: coordinates of the map corner(s) or centre, plus map dimensions.

Reason: what recording location enables
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Enables spatial reconstruction and co-registration with other analytical images.
Mass (mg) of solid material digested or volume (mL) of liquid taken for dissolution.

Reason: what the value is used for
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Used for yield calculations and concentration back-calculation.
Total number of distinct acid digestion steps required to dissolve the sample.

Some procedures require multiple sequential steps — for example, an initial open-beaker HF–HNO3 dissolution followed by a second closed-vessel step for residues retaining refractory minerals, or by an aqua regia reflux to destroy fluoride complexes.
Type of vessel used for acid digestion.

Reason: why vessel type constrains what can be dissolved
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Vessel type constrains maximum temperature and pressure and determines suitability for refractory mineral dissolution (e.g., Parr bombs required for complete silicate digestion at high temperatures).
Acid mixture used for sample dissolution.
Record acid type(s) and concentration(s) where known (e.g., concentrated HF–HNO3 in Parr bombs is standard for silicate dissolution).

Reason: why complete dissolution matters for isotope-ratio work
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For isotope-ratio work, complete matrix dissolution is required to avoid isotopic fractionation during partial dissolution.
Temperature at which acid digestion was carried out (°C).

Reason: 'procedure specifies the target' restates the procedure-level tier
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the target temperature.
Duration of the primary acid digestion step (hours or days).
Whether chromatographic separation of element groups (e.g., using ion exchange resin) was performed prior to analysis.

Reason: why separation is performed
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Separation may be required to remove matrix elements that cause variable mass bias, to eliminate isobaric interferences, or to isolate an element group before measurement (e.g., Fe and Cu–Zn for isotope dilution, Hf separation from REE, removal of Cr and Ni from Fe fractions).

Reason: when it is mandatory vs optional — technique scope, not our Column C (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: It is usually mandatory for isotope-ratio procedures and optional for concentration measurement.
Record resin type and elution matrix conditions if applied.
Record 'None' if the direct digestion solution is analyzed.
Isotopic spike material added to the sample before or during digestion for isotope dilution (ID) analysis or double-spike mass bias correction.

Reason: requirement to spike before digestion, plus the reason
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For double-spike procedures, the spike must be added and equilibrated before digestion to correct for any isotopic fractionation during dissolution and column chemistry.
For concentration ID, the spike must be added before digestion for complete equilibration.
Record spike name or certificate reference, spike isotopes, and whether added pre- or post-digestion.
Record 'None' if ID or double-spike technique is not used.
Acid type and concentration of the final dissolved sample solution introduced to the instrument.

Reason: what the matrix affects
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Directly affects instrument response and ion transmission.

Reason: matching requirement plus the reason for it
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For isotope-ratio procedures, acid molarity must be precisely matched between samples and bracketing standards to avoid matrix-induced mass bias offsets.
Procedures targeting HFSE may add trace HF to the final solution to keep those elements in solution.
Type and material of the pneumatic nebulizer used for sample introduction.

Reason: what nebulizer choice affects
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Affects droplet size distribution and sample introduction efficiency.

Field: Spray Chamber Type and Cooling Temperature
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Type of spray chamber and cooling temperature if thermostatted (°C).

Field: Spray Chamber Type and Cooling Temperature
Reason: what chamber and temperature control
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Chamber type and temperature control aerosol droplet size and the solvent vapor load reaching the plasma.

Field: Spray Chamber Type and Cooling Temperature
Reason: why a chamber is sometimes placed downstream
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: In some procedures a spray chamber is placed downstream of a desolvating nebulizer to improve signal stability.
Desolvating nebulizer or membrane desolvator used upstream of the plasma to reduce solvent load.

Reason: what desolvation achieves and when it is used
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Lowers oxide production rates and increases sensitivity, and is commonly used for low-abundance analytes or small sample sizes.

Reason: the mass-bias trade-off
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Note the trade-off: desolvation can introduce additional instrumental mass bias instability relative to wet plasma introduction.
Record 'None' if not used.
Peristaltic pump speed or self-aspiration flow rate for sample introduction (µL/min or mL/min).
Flow rate of the carrier argon gas delivered through the nebulizer (L/min).

Reason: what the flow controls
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Controls aerosol transport and strongly influences signal sensitivity and stability.

Reason: 'adjusted daily' restates D=Editable
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Adjusted daily to optimize signal.
Duration of instrument rinse between successive sample solutions (seconds).

Reason: what wash time controls
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Controls carryover and memory effects.

Reason: why washout is critical for isotope-ratio work
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For isotope-ratio work, complete washout is critical to prevent cross-contamination between samples with differing isotopic compositions.
Target concentration of internal standard element(s) in all measured solutions (µg/L or ppb).
Record 'N/A' where Internal Standard Element is 'None'.
Reactor and irradiation position used to convert 39K to 39Ar, the irradiation duration, and whether cadmium shielding or sample rotation was used.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by Schaen et al. (2021).

Reason: why shielding and rotation matter — they propagate into J and every age
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Shielding and rotation determine the neutron energy spectrum and fluence gradient across the package, both of which propagate directly into J and hence into every age.

Reason: a library roadmap note about a future module; not content for a researcher filling the field
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Note: fission-track dating by the external detector method has an equivalent requirement (Kohn et al. 2024, 'Irradiation reactor'), so this is a candidate for generalisation once a second irradiation-based system module exists.
Correction factors for argon isotopes produced during irradiation from potassium, calcium and chlorine rather than from the decay of 40K, with the reference for each.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by Schaen et al. (2021).

Distinct from spectral or isobaric interference in the mass spectrometer: these are nuclear production reactions occurring in the reactor, and the correction factors are properties of the irradiation facility, not of the instrument.

Reason: roadmap note — 'candidate for a future general interference module'
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Candidate for a future general interference module.
How argon was released from the sample: for incremental heating, the temperature or laser power of each step and its duration; for total fusion, the fusion conditions.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by Schaen et al. (2021).

Reason: why the schedule governs how an age spectrum is read
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The schedule determines which diffusion domains contribute to each step and therefore how an age spectrum should be read.

Reason: roadmap note about a future stepped-heating module
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Note: (U-Th)/He and continuous ramped heating have equivalent requirements (Flowers et al. 2024), so this is a candidate for generalisation once a stepped-heating system module exists.
The corrected ratio of radiogenic 40Ar to potassium-derived 39Ar, with its uncertainty — the measured quantity from which the date is calculated once multiplied by J.

Reason: provenance plus why reporting F enables recomputation
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by Schaen et al. (2021), who note that reporting it lets a reader recompute dates against any future revision of the monitor age or decay constants without returning to the raw isotope data.

Annealing and partial-dissolution conditions applied to mitigate Pb loss before analysis, following Mattinson (2005): annealing temperature and duration, and the acid, temperature and duration of the partial-dissolution step.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Condon et al. (2024) require these where chemical abrasion was applied, and state that it generally should be for zircon.
